title: A Lagrangian heuristic for robustness, with an application to train timetabling
contribution: Shows that a minor modification of the Caprara-Fischetti-Toth Lagrangian heuristic for train timetabling (buffer prizes in the objective whose weight grows along the subgradient iterations, every intermediate solution kept) yields robust corridor timetables that dominate 13 of 18 solutions of the FSZ light-robustness method on Trenitalia instances in much shorter computing time (pp. 7-13).
problem_entry: Robust approaches enlarge the model, multiply computing time and force rewrites of nominal software; the entry is that the Lagrangian scheme is 'natively' suited to robustness once two features are added (abstract p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: Artificial prizes on station-arc buffers (capped at 15 minutes, weighted by position along the path) with a weight F_k raised during subgradient optimization (0.1, then 0.5 after 900 iterations, then +0.5 every 100 until above 2.0); all heuristic solutions kept as an approximate Pareto set, selected per efficiency threshold by a robustness sum and validated offline (pp. 7-10).
assumptions: Aperiodic TTP on one one-way corridor (for comparability with FSZ and its validation tool), binary arc variables on a discretized time-space graph with clique capacity constraints relaxed in Lagrangian fashion (node-variable form in the code), fixed travel times so buffers are stop extensions; validation assumes all trains scheduled and fixed precedences (pp. 4-8).
proof_devices: Subgradient optimization with a pool of recently violated clique constraints; a constructive heuristic on Lagrangian profits and a rescheduling local search at every iteration, pp. 7-8
Weight schedule F_k for the robustness term: efficiency first, robustness later, p. 8
Position weight (1 - e^(-lambda p))(len(t) - p) on buffer prizes after Kroon et al., M = 15, lambda = 3, p. 8
Quadratic robustness sum (9) used only for a-posteriori selection; its linearizations inside the loop did worse than the linear proxy (6), p. 9
Selection rule fixed in advance: per efficiency threshold 99/95/90% validate only the solution of smallest robustness sum, p. 9; Algorithm 1 RobuLag, p. 10
experiments: Six Trenitalia corridor instances (41-400 trains, Table 1 p. 11) plus combined 500-1,000-train instances; arms: nominal Lagrangian heuristic and FSZ (CPLEX 11.0, 2 h + 2 h) run by the authors; C on a Pentium IV 3.2 GHz; robustness = average total delay from the FSZ simulation tool; FSZ solutions dominated 13/18, 13/18 strictly at 1,200 s (opposite once) and 14/18 on large instances; robust runs cost 2.3-4.1 times the nominal CPU time (my ratios, Table 2); single runs, no seeds (pp. 10-15).
positioning: Borrows the robustness measure and validation tool of FSZ 2009 and the slack idea of Light Robustness, reviews stochastic, recoverable and genetic approaches to robust TTP, and claims novelty only for the Lagrangian adaptation (pp. 2-4).
writing: Proof-of-concept framing with an explicit modest-purpose sentence before the main comparison (p. 11) and a statement of what the paper does not attempt, a new concept of robustness (p. 2).
limits_future: The adaptation had to be carefully defined for this problem and its generality is left out of scope (p. 3); FSZ may not cancel trains while RobuLag may (p. 12); future: other classes, networks with detours, rolling stock, station routing, multi-objective Lagrangian heuristics (pp. 13-14).

method_links.note: smallest-code step outside MIP: robustness added by a minor modification of an existing Lagrangian heuristic instead of a larger robust model and new software; the expensive validator stays outside the loop

for a heuristic the rougher model wins, in the objective rather than the variables: the linear buffer-prize proxy stays in the loop, the finer quadratic robustness sum only selects, after its linearizations did worse

rival is the group's FSZ code run by the authors, with the reference nominal value aligned to FSZ's first phase; but the arms differ in allowed actions (train cancellations) and budget, and dominance counts come from single runs

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Weight sweep harvests a Pareto set
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the robustness weight F_k is raised on a fixed schedule within one subgradient run and every heuristic solution is kept, so one run returns solutions with different efficiency-robustness trade-offs for later validation

transferable: To add a second criterion to an iterative heuristic, put it into the objective with a weight raised on a fixed schedule (here after 900 iterations, then every 100) and keep every solution produced; one run returns a trade-off set instead of one point (pp. 8, 10).

Keep the in-loop proxy linear and cheap; evaluate the real criterion offline with the expensive tool only on solutions picked by a rule fixed in advance (one per efficiency threshold, smallest robustness sum) (pp. 8-9).
When the rival defines its own reference value, re-run your method with the rival's reference so that thresholds mean the same in both arms (p. 12).
Report dominance counts against the rival at two budgets and on scaled-up instances (pp. 12-15).

quotes.text: our purpose here is not to show that our approach outperforms all the methods for robust TTP available in the literature, but rather to show that, although it is a straightforward simple-minded modification of an existing approach for the nominal case, it yields comparable (in fact, better) results
Note that the adaptation of the Lagrangian optimization scheme to deal with robustness had to be carefully defined for the specific problem at hand.

title: Cutting plane versus compact formulations for uncertain (integer) linear programs
contribution: Not carded: the file is not this work but 'Robustness by cutting planes and the Uncertain Set Covering Problem' by Fischetti and Monaci, a preliminary draft dated 25 May 2009 (19 pp., homepage file Uncertain_SCP.pdf); it should be registered as its own work row before it is carded.

title: Approximating the Split Closure
contribution: A hybrid split-closure approximation that plugs lift-and-project separation (elementary and two-variable non-elementary disjunctions, with a cache of failure certificates) and two-row aggregation into the relax-and-cut GMI backbone, closing 71.2% of the integrality gap on MIPLIB 3.0 in 3.28 s (exact closure about 80%) and 55.2% on MIPLIB 2003 in 110.09 s, and helping CPLEX solve a1c1s1 and sp97ar (pp. 20-23).
problem_entry: The split closure is very tight (about 80% of the gap closed on MIPLIB 3.0) but exact separation is NP-hard and unacceptably slow; existing heuristic separators have complementary strengths and none dominates, so combine them in a sound way (pp. 2, 11).
key_idea: Relax-and-cut (GMI cuts read from near-optimal primal-feasible Lagrangian bases during subgradient) as backbone for its speed and numerical stability, with lift-and-project over violated elementary disjunctions after each main iteration, two-variable +-1 disjunctions when those fail, and brute-force two-row aggregation; Theorem 1 shows that integer row combinations of possibly infeasible bases are needed to reach the split closure (pp. 4-11, 18).
assumptions: MIP in standard form with integer and continuous variables; P bounded and nonempty for the Lagrangian dual; test set MIPLIB 3.0 (54) and MIPLIB 2003 (20) after removing instances where one GMI round does not improve the bound or no integer solution is known, following Dash and Goycoolea (pp. 1, 4, 12).
proof_devices: New short constructive proof of Theorem 1 (Andersen et al. 2005) via Bonami (2010): an extra free integer variable x_{n+1} = pi x makes the split elementary, and the CGLP basis structure yields an integral combination of the tableau rows of a basis of A, pp. 8-9

Eight-step GMI separator: basis refactor, support-only row computation, dense-row discard, closest-bound complementing, integral slacks, back-substitution, dense or high-dynamism cut discard, pp. 14-15

Cut pool: efficacy at least 1e-4, orthogonality cosine 0.1, dynamism above 1e10 discarded, thresholds lowered when model dynamism exceeds 1e7, caps of 1 GB and 10x rows with purges by efficacy and age, p. 13
Tailing-off termination: relative bound gain below 1e-3 for 3 iterations, at most 100 iterations, p. 15
Cache of lines from failed CGLPs (certificate pair y, z with step interval) to skip disjunctions without solving their CGLP, p. 19
Aggregation restricted to pairs of fractional integer basic rows, computed on S, at most 10 partners per row, p. 20
experiments: C++ with CPLEX 12.2 as LP black box, Intel Core i5 2.66 GHz, one CPU per process, 1 h per instance; shifted geometric means (shift 0.1) for time and arithmetic means for gap closed; rc vs the earlier fast/faster, own L&P vs Bonami's published figures from a roughly equivalent machine, mix variants, a single-thread CPLEX B&C row labelled unfair; four hard instances (selected by CPLEX above 10 min and mix+aggr above 70% gap closed) with cuts added to 4-core CPLEX, 10 h; single runs, no seeds (pp. 12-23).
positioning: Merges relax-and-cut (own 2011), lift-and-project (Balas et al.; Bonami 2010), reduce-and-split (Andersen et al.; Cornuejols and Nannicini) and brute-force aggregation (Dey et al.); credits Dash et al. 2011 for an independently developed CGLP-skip check (pp. 2-11, 19).
writing: Survey-first structure that recasts each separator as fixing either the split or the multipliers (p. 3); implementation details get their own subsection (pp. 13-15); averages only, 'to improve readability' (p. 12); a candid label on the unfair comparison (p. 21).
limits_future: Aggressive cuts pay only on very hard instances where they close much gap (p. 22); MIPLIB 3.0 now too easy (p. 21); the cache saves 40% of CGLPs but only about 20% of the time (p. 20); aggregation doubles the time on MIPLIB 2003 (p. 21); timtab2 not closed (p. 23); no future directions stated (p. 23).

method_links.note: the loop is redesigned and the separator kept: ordinary GMI cuts read from bases sampled along a subgradient trajectory instead of only the large-LP optimum, and a fixed iteration count replaced by tailing-off detection

step 4, the ceiling: the approximation is placed against the exact closure's gap closed from the literature ('less than 9% away'); the solver stays a black box for the LPs and receives the slack cuts in its own pool

dated lapse, mitigated: the hard-MIP class keeps only instances where mix+aggr itself closes more than 70% of the gap (fails the swap test), and the own lift-and-project code is compared with Bonami's published figures from 'roughly equivalent machines'; the claim is limited to '(some) hard MIPs' and the CPLEX row is labelled unfair

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Failure certificates as a skip cache
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: every failed CGLP leaves a certificate pair (y, z), stored as a line through x* with its step interval; later disjunctions whose split interval lies inside it are skipped without solving their CGLP; the cache is cleared when x* changes
the scalable, numerically stable relax-and-cut is chosen as backbone and complementary separators are called at fixed points of its loop, because no single separator dominates

transferable: Keep the certificate of a failed separation (the pair y, z of a failed CGLP as a line through x* with its step interval) and skip later disjunctions it already rules out; clear the cache when x* changes (p. 19).
Replace a fixed number of cut rounds by tailing-off detection relative to the initial gap (below 1e-3 for 3 consecutive iterations, at most 100) (p. 15).
Test a GMI cut's violation on the variables of S before computing the whole cut; cap cuts per basis (200) and primal simplex iterations per subgradient step (1,000) (pp. 15-16).

To test a separator inside a solver, keep the cuts tight at the end of the loop in the formulation and pass the slack ones to the solver's cut pool; add a run with the optimal solution given upfront to remove heuristic variability (p. 22).
Print the ceiling (the exact closure) and a full-solver row labelled as not comparable next to the method's numbers (p. 21).

quotes.text: This is by no means a fair comparison, as Cplex does not implement a pure rank-1 cutting-plane algorithm, but is free to use any machinery

Actually, our computational experience shows that not only the instance must be very hard for an aggressive cut generator to be worthwhile, but the gap closed by cutting planes must be significant to really speedup enumeration.

title: Alberto Caprara (1968-2012): Scientific Contributions
contribution: An eleven-author commemorative OPTIMA survey, compiled by Andrea Lodi, of Alberto Caprara's contributions in integer programming, knapsack, bin packing, computational biology and railway applications; among them it records the Caprara-Fischetti-Toth Lagrangian set-covering heuristic CFT that won the FASTER competition and the corridor train-timetabling model (pp. 1-9).
problem_entry: An invitation by the OPTIMA editors to devote the issue to Caprara, used to write a paper outlining his contributions in five areas (p. 1); not a research entry.
key_idea: One section per area: general-purpose cuts ({0,1/2} and mod-k separation, split-cut separation complexity), special-purpose cuts, Lagrangian relaxation and other methods (pp. 1-2); knapsack, bin packing and computational biology (pp. 3-8); railway crew planning, timetabling, platforming and train-unit assignment (pp. 8-9).
proof_devices: CFT recalled: subgradient, heuristic and refining-and-fixing phases; a core problem of columns updated by variable pricing, p. 8
Lagrangian reduced costs fix set-covering variables at zero before branch-and-bound in the exact code, p. 2
Quadratic knapsack relaxed into independent continuous knapsacks inside branch-and-bound, p. 2
Caprara's negative result: a natural ILP for certain partitioning problems has a weak, trivial LP bound even with all cuts of a kind, favouring Dantzig-Wolfe or Lagrangian methods, p. 2
experiments: none (results recalled in prose, e.g. CFT's best known values on all instances and quadratic knapsacks with up to 400 binaries, p. 2)
positioning: A commemorative survey in a collective voice; credits Caprara with settling open problems (split-cut separation complexity, sorting by reversals) and lists his prizes and competition wins (pp. 2, 5, 8).
writing: Topic-by-topic overview by many contributors compiled by Lodi (p. 1), in a celebratory register ('a real breakthrough', p. 2); no section is signed.
limits_future: Records one open problem, the worst-case ratio between guillotine and unrestricted two-dimensional bin packing (between 4/3 and T-infinity, pp. 4-5); a farewell section (p. 9); no limits stated.

method_links.note: retrospective account in a collective voice: CFT runs on a core problem of columns kept current by Lagrangian pricing, called one of the main ingredients of its success, and the exact set-covering code fixes variables by Lagrangian reduced costs before branching; both are Caprara-Fischetti-Toth papers (refs. 28-29)

transferable: When a set-covering-type model is too large for the Lagrangian loop, run the loop on a core subset of columns and update the core by Lagrangian reduced-cost pricing (p. 8).
In an exact code, use Lagrangian reduced costs to fix variables at zero before entering branch-and-bound (p. 2).
coauthors: Nikhil Bansal, Giuseppe Lancia, Adam N. Letchford, Andrea Lodi, Michele Monaci, Ulrich Pferschy, David Pisinger, Juan-José Salazar-González, Maxim Sviridenko, Paolo Toth

quotes.text: We are very grateful to Andrea Lodi who compiled multiple contributions of many of Alberto’s colleagues into a comprehensive overview.
The use of pricing within Lagrangian optimization drastically reduced the computing time, and was one of the main ingredients for the success of the overall CFT scheme.

title: Self-splitting of workload in parallel computation
contribution: SelfSplit: a deterministic, almost communication-free way to parallelize a sequential tree search in which every worker repeats the same sampling phase and then processes only the nodes of its own color, giving near-linear speedups up to 64 workers on Gecode CP instances (pp. 3-9).
problem_entry: Parallel tree search needs load balancing by work stealing or a master, with communication and synchronization that hurt scalability and slow the deterministic variants; modify a given deterministic sequential code so that each worker decides alone what to process (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Each worker reads the whole input plus (k, K), runs the same deterministic sampling phase, then keeps only the open nodes of color k (pseudo-random colors, or a paused-node queue colored round-robin by sorted difficulty scores); balance is statistical, with many more subproblems than workers; results merged at the end (pp. 3-6).
assumptions: A deterministic original algorithm (or coloring right after a synchronization point if it is parallel), small input and output, sampling and merge not bottlenecks; tests on Gecode examples that are infeasible or enumerate all solutions, some with symmetry breaking added (pp. 2, 4-5, 8).
proof_devices: Coverage: each node is processed by at least one worker, p. 5
Difficulty estimate log2 of the Cartesian product of domains vs. the root (free variables for binaries), with range lists for integer and a capped count for set variables, pp. 6-7
Pause threshold theta = 10 (1,024-fold reduction); if |S| < 2000 after sampling, double theta and restart, p. 8
Implementation as a custom Gecode propagator that stores the node and fails, compatible with copy and recomputation, pp. 6-7
experiments: Gecode 4.0, K in {1, 4, 16, 64}, one thread per worker for determinism and reproducibility, ten instances; speedup at K = 64 from 36.63 (ortholatin 5) to 61.34 (golomb 14); one parameter setting for all instances; hardware not stated, no repeated runs (pp. 8-9).
positioning: Against MapReduce and work stealing (pp. 1-2); next to Regin et al.'s embarrassingly parallel search and Moisan et al.'s parallel LDS, stating the differences (master process, dynamic assignment, nondeterminism, LDS-specific split) (pp. 2, 5).
writing: Short conference paper: four claimed features listed up front (p. 2), a proof-of-concept implementation (p. 7), and six future variants in the conclusions (pp. 10-11).
limits_future: Unsuitable for solvers that learn global information during the search, though MIP codes gather cuts, pseudocosts and incumbents during sampling (pp. 9-10); legacy ATSP speedups reported without numbers (p. 9); future: fewer workers than colors as a heuristic or a time estimate, pause and resume, incumbent sharing, failure handling, redundant colors (pp. 10-11).

method_links.note: step 3, the smallest code: the change needs a few lines, is written as a propagator because a search engine was harder, and about 10 new lines parallelized two legacy FORTRAN ATSP codes
steps 3 and 5: one parameter setting on very different instances, and the test-set restriction (infeasible or all-solutions instances) stated with its reason
variability removed by construction (deterministic single-thread workers) rather than measured; no seeds or spread reported

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Redundant deterministic prefix instead of communication
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: all workers repeat the same sampling phase, so the global information gathered there (in MIP: cuts, pseudocosts, incumbent) is shared without messages and the split needs no coordination

transferable: Parallelize a deterministic tree search by adding (k, K), a sampling flag, a deterministic node coloring and a rule that skips other colors (pp. 4-5).
Color paused nodes by sorting difficulty estimates and dealing them round-robin; restart with a doubled threshold if too few nodes were paused (pp. 6, 8).
Measure scaling only on infeasible or enumerate-all instances, one thread per worker (p. 8).
Run fewer workers than colors to bound the K-worker time from below and to estimate the sequential time as Ts + K*T (p. 10).

quotes.text: Note that, despite the fact that our instances are very different, we used exactly the same parameter tuning on all of them, showing that the method is quite robust.

Therefore, performing the sampling phase redundantly in parallel by all workers has the advantage of sharing a potentially big amount of global information without communication—a distinguishing feature of SelfSplit.

title: MIP‐and‐refine matheuristic for smart grid energy management
contribution: A case study showing that a simple multi-start greedy feeding all its solutions to CPLEX's off-the-shelf polishing (MIP-and-refine) beats CPLEX alone and CPLEX plus polishing by a large amount on smart-home appliance scheduling MIPs for which CPLEX struggles even to find a feasible solution (pp. 14-16).
problem_entry: Black-box MIP refinement needs no ad hoc work but lacks good or even feasible solutions to refine, and appliance-scheduling MIPs are very hard to solve without hints from a heuristic (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Two ingredients only: a MIP model and a fast multi-start greedy on a restricted problem; the greedy's diversified solutions seed the solver's polishing, so the two complementary modules work together (pp. 2-4, 14, 16-17).
assumptions: Appliances as sequences of uninterruptible phases with energy totals and per-slot power bounds, user time windows, time-varying grid price and peak power, one PV source and one battery; MIP with binaries x, s, t per phase and slot and battery binaries, linearized battery curves; 60 random instances (96 slots, 4 scenario sets, 10/20/30 appliances, 5 per cell) (pp. 4-12).
proof_devices: Greedy: appliances by nonincreasing total energy, all start shifts of the first phase, best slot for each next phase within its delay window, on a restricted problem with constant phase duration and energy, pp. 10-11; Algorithm 1, p. 13
Time complexity O(N n_max D_max d_max m), pp. 11-12
Multi-start by shifting the priority vector, N runs, pp. 10, 14
Polishing after the root for 10 nodes with all cuts disabled, seeded with all greedy solutions, p. 14
experiments: CPLEX 12.4, all arms single-thread: Greedy-alone, multi-start Greedy, Cplex (default, stopped at first feasible), Cplex+Polish, Greedy+Polish; % cost change vs Greedy-alone (arithmetic mean over 5 instances, % std), times, proven optima marked; Greedy+Polish best by a large amount (e.g. -21.2% in 617.7 s where Cplex needs 46,439.1 s for its first solution); hardware not stated, no seeds (pp. 14-16).
positioning: Builds on Rothberg's evolutionary polishing and on the appliance models of Sou et al. and Barbato et al.; no comparison with the smart-grid heuristics it cites (pp. 2-4, 16).
writing: A Prologue states the general message before the application (pp. 2-3); the claims are hedged twice ('we cannot claim', pp. 3, 16).
limits_future: No deep theoretical contribution claimed (p. 3); no claim against sophisticated heuristics from the literature without more comparisons (p. 16); the greedy ignores the batteries that the MIP exploits (p. 16); future: other very difficult problem classes (p. 17).

method_links.note: steps 1 and 3: the stock solver first as a black box (to first feasible), then with its built-in polishing, then the authors' greedy feeding the same polishing; the refinement is used off the shelf, not reimplemented
simplicity of both ingredients rather than thinning by projection: the model need not be sophisticated because the refinement resizes it, and the greedy runs on a restricted problem
steps 1 and 4: the two refine arms share the polishing settings and differ only in their starting solutions; every arm single-thread

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the heuristic need not be effective; its role is to fill a pool of feasible solutions for the polisher, the more diversified the better; Greedy+Polish beats Cplex+Polish partly because several diversified solutions are passed

transferable: Before writing a custom metaheuristic, give every solution of a fast multi-start greedy to the solver's own polishing (few nodes, cuts off) (pp. 14, 16).
Lay out the evaluation as nested arms that add one ingredient at a time: greedy alone, multi-start greedy, solver to first feasible, solver plus polishing, greedy plus polishing (p. 14).
Keep the greedy fast by solving a restricted version of the problem (fixed phase durations and energies) and leave the rest to the MIP (pp. 10-11).

quotes.text: The heuristic needs not to be very effective, as its role is just to initialize a pool of feasible solutions–the more diversified the better.
Of course, we cannot claim that Greedy+Polish would outperform more sophisticated heuristic approaches from the literature on similar problems

title: On handling indicator constraints in mixed integer programming
contribution: Shows on ramp-loss SVM instances that a global solver on the nonconvex complementary reformulation beats commercial MIQP solvers on the big-M model, isolates aggressive bound tightening and iterative McCormick strengthening as the reason, and transplants them into CPLEX as local implied bound cuts (15 of 23 solved against 1) and iterative domain reduction (all 23 in under a minute) (pp. 6-16).
problem_entry: Big-M constraints give weak relaxations and numerical trouble; an empirical and surprising observation (Couenne on the nonconvex reformulation beats every MIQP solver on the big-M model) is the entry (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: Dissect why the GO solver wins (bound reduction and per-node McCormick strengthening, confirmed by switching each off), then give MILP the same ingredient online (locally valid big-M recomputed per node via CPLEX local implied bound cuts) or a priori (iterative domain reduction by node-limited min/max MILPs under the cutoff) (pp. 7-14).
assumptions: Convex MIQP with big-M constraints vs the nonconvex complementary MINLP; Proposition 2.1 (local optima of the continuous relaxation are mixed binary); 23 artificial TypeB instances of Brooks, n = 100, d = 2, chosen to control data and size (pp. 4-5).
proof_devices: Proposition 2.1 by contradiction: a fractional z-bar_i can be raised to 1 keeping feasibility with a lower objective, p. 5
McCormick linearization of u_i = theta_i z-bar_i: Couenne builds its own big-M with per-row bounds, p. 7
Objective-cutoff bound omega_i in [-sqrt(2U), sqrt(2U)], FBBT and probing, pp. 9-11; bound-update formulas for omega, b, xi, p. 12
Ablations on Couenne: McCormick cuts only at the root, bound reduction off, both worsen performance dramatically, pp. 11-12
Control experiments: three MIQP solvers on the big-M model (p. 6) and an L1-norm objective that removes the MIQP extension from the comparison (p. 9)
Iterative domain reduction: node-limited (10k) MILPs min/max omega_i and b under the cutoff U from a 100k-node run, cycled until no bound improves, p. 14
experiments: Intel Xeon E3-1220V2 3.10 GHz, 1 h; Couenne (CouenneClassifier branch) solves 22/23 vs IBM-Cplex 0 (Gurobi and Xpress similar), Couenne with continuous branching 23/23; CPLEX 12.6.1 with 4 threads: default 1/23, local implied bound cuts 15/23, iterative domain reduction 23/23 in under a minute (average below 30 s and 150k nodes); single runs, no seeds; Table 1 thread count not stated (pp. 5-16).
positioning: Against the common practice of big-M plus MILP when logical constraints are the only nonconvexity (p. 2); builds on Brooks's ramp-loss model and Couenne's bound-reduction machinery, with Bonami et al. for the theory (pp. 2, 4, 9-11).
writing: Surprise as structure: raw results, 'Why are these results surprising?', the reasons, the fix (p. 3, sections 3-6); 'To our pleasant surprise' (p. 15).
limits_future: One class of 23 instances with n = 100 (p. 5), 'a special class of classification problems' (p. 15); validity detail of the node-limited bound MILPs not stated (p. 14); future: other MINLP ingredients for MILP (p. 16).

method_links.note: steps 1-2: stock solvers on the model as given (CPLEX, Gurobi, Xpress; Couenne out of the box), then a built-in CPLEX feature at a very aggressive setting, then own preprocessing stating the critical sub-decision (variable bounds) as auxiliary node-limited MILPs solved by the same solver
step 5 subtraction applied to a rival's code: the winning solver's components switched off one at a time until removal hurts
alternative explanations removed before the claim: three MIQP solvers on the big-M model and an L1 objective that takes the MIQP extension out; cross-code comparison conceded to be hard; no seeds

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Dissect the surprising winner, transplant the ingredient
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: an unexpected solver win is taken apart component by component (McCormick separation at nodes, bound reduction) with controls, and the active ingredient is then built into the mainstream MILP solver in two forms

transferable: When a solver that is expected to lose wins, switch its components off one at a time on your instances and run a control that removes the obvious confound (here an L1 objective) before transplanting anything (pp. 9, 11-12).

Transplant a bound-tightening ingredient into MILP in two forms and report both: online local cuts (a big-M recomputed per node from the local bounds) and a priori domain reduction by node-limited min and max MILPs under the cutoff, repeated until no bound moves (pp. 13-14).
Bound free continuous variables from the objective cutoff (here omega_i in [-sqrt(2U), sqrt(2U)]) before building any relaxation (p. 10).
coauthors: Pietro Belotti, Pierre Bonami, Andrea Lodi, Michele Monaci, Amaya Nogales-Gómez, Domenico Salvagnin

quotes.text: More generally, we argue that aggressive bound tightening is often overlooked in MILP, while it represents a significant building block for enhancing MILP technology when indicator constraints and disjunctive terms are present.

Through a careful analysis of Couenne’s features and components we have been able to isolate those that make a difference, namely aggressive bound tightening and iterative strengthening of the McCormick linearization.

title: Proximity Benders: a decomposition heuristic for stochastic programs
contribution: Proximity Benders: proximity search applied to the Benders master (Hamming objective, soft cutoff, black-box MILP master, slack-augmented second stages, a repair heuristic), which gives the lowest primal integral and the most wins at 1 h on stochastic network interdiction and 2,000-scenario network design instances, while CPLEX wins at 1 h on the easier facility-location set (pp. 3-12).
problem_entry: Benders converges too slowly to serve as a heuristic on huge stochastic programs; proximity search is primal and complements it; target instances are too big to load or have a prohibitive root LP (abstract p. 1; p. 2).
key_idea: Replace the master objective by the Hamming distance to the incumbent with a soft cutoff, solve the master by any black-box MILP solver, derive feasibility or optimality cuts from slack-augmented second stages, and recenter when an improving feasible point appears; the nesting reverses local branching inside Benders (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Binary first stage and LP second stages in block structure, an easy initial feasible solution; monotone feasibility for the repair; instances from Bodur et al. (facility location, network interdiction) and Crainic et al. network design with 2,000 generated scenarios (pp. 3, 5-6, 8, 10).
proof_devices: Soft cutoff with a variable z0 of large cost M0 on the master, proximity search with incumbent, pp. 2-3
Slack-augmented second-stage LPs (z_k, nu_k) after Fischetti, Salvagnin and Zanette 2010, giving feasibility or optimality cuts, pp. 3-4; Algorithm 2, p. 4
Repair heuristic under monotone feasibility, raising y through auxiliary problems, pp. 4-5; Algorithm 3, p. 5
Non-aggressive minimum improvement theta = 1e-5 times the incumbent value, decreasing, p. 5
experiments: C with CPLEX 12.6.1, single thread, 1 h, Intel Xeon E3-1220V2 3.10 GHz, 16 GB; arms Cplex default, a Benders arm (its description lost in the text) and ProxyBenders; primal integral, wins, improved instances and improving solutions at 100/600/3,600 s; Cplex wins most at 1 h on facility location; ProxyBenders has the lowest PI and most wins at 1 h on interdiction and network design (21 wins, PI 163.78 vs Cplex 236.75); single runs, no seeds (pp. 5-11).
positioning: Relates to LNS and local branching (p. 1), reverses Rei et al.'s local branching inside Benders (p. 4), and notes a similarity with the feasibility pump (p. 12).
writing: Proof-of-concept framing; the method-of-choice claim is scoped to very large stochastic programs (pp. 2, 12) and one test set is conceded to be inadequate (p. 6).
limits_future: Proof-of-concept, not tailored to a problem (p. 12); facility-location instances inadequate to show the benefit (p. 6); future: sensitivity to the initial solution, more aggressive theta schemes, cut management, partial second-stage solves, randomization as in the feasibility pump, parallelization (p. 12).

method_links.note: step 3, change the master objective: the cut recipe is kept, the master objective becomes a proximity function, which changes the master points and therefore the Benders cuts
the modified master can be solved by any black-box MILP solver; proximity search runs the solver as a black box
the facility-location set on which Cplex wins at 1 h is kept and printed, but the next sets are introduced as more appropriate to show the benefits, within the scope stated at the start
dated lapse: heuristics compared by primal integral from one run per instance and arm, without seeds; randomization only named as future work, credited to the feasibility pump

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: instead of local search inside a Benders method, a black-box Benders solver runs inside an outer local search (proximity search as a tactical tool to drive Benders)

transferable: Turn a Benders code into a heuristic by changing only the master: Hamming objective to the incumbent and a soft cutoff (a variable with a large cost), cuts from slack-augmented second-stage problems (pp. 3-4).
When raising first-stage variables preserves feasibility, repair infeasible first-stage solutions by raising components through auxiliary problems (p. 5).
Compare heuristics by primal integral at several time limits plus win and improving-solution counts, with the best known value as reference when optima are unknown (pp. 5-6, 10).
coauthors: Natashia Boland, Michele Monaci, Martin Savelsbergh

quotes.text: However, our approach reverses the role of local search and Benders decomposition: instead of using local search inside a Benders method, we apply a black-box Benders solver within an external local search scheme, i.e., PS.
The results above are encouraging and demonstrate the potential of Proximity Benders, but the instances are inadequate to fully reveal the power of Proximity Benders.
